title: Geneva: A Dynamic Confluence of Speculative Execution and In-Order Commitment Windows
problem: Out-of-order microprocessors expand ROB and IQ resources for memory-level parallelism, but this expansion incurs significant cost and energy trade-offs. Larger buffers improve MLP but increase power consumption and silicon area.
motivation: Efficiently balancing memory-level parallelism against power and area budgets is critical for modern processor design.
method: Geneva reallocates a portion of the reorder buffer as a dynamic queue (DQ) that can serve as an ROB, instruction queue, or both depending on runtime operational needs. The architecture dynamically adjusts how the shared queue resources are partitioned between speculative execution and in-order commitment based on workload behavior.
key_novelty: A dynamic queue that flexibly multiplexes reorder buffer storage between commit-window and dispatch-queue functions based on operational demand.
contributions: Dynamic queue microarchitecture enabling adaptive resource sharing between ROB and IQ
15.6% energy savings through reduced resource allocation
2.6% performance improvement over conventional out-of-order cores
Hardware-efficient approach to memory-level parallelism without fixed expansion
limitations: Limitations, constraints on dynamic allocation, and workload-specific behavior are not discussed in the abstract.
primary_theme: dynamic resource multiplexing in out-of-order cores
